source.title: Revealing the Learning Dynamics of Long-Context Continual Pre-training
source.authors: Yupu Liang; Shuang Chen; Guan-Wei Zhang; Shaolei Wang; Sun-Cong Zheng

record.file_problem: The text includes the full paper through the appendix, but the Abstract heading is followed by no abstract text in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It measures perplexity and downstream performance across LCCP training-token checkpoints, addressing token-scale trends with different measures and in a long-context continual-pretraining setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports token-count trends for PPL and downstream benchmarks, and correlations between NIAH metrics and downstream results. It does not report parameter-count or compute sweeps, compute-optimal allocations, or comparisons of architectures. Retrieval-head correlations are not rows because those metrics are not loss, scale, or downstream performance as specified by the claim versions.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, long-context continual pretraining (LCCP) of one 80B-total MoE model, it reports held-out PPL and SFT-probe downstream scores at checkpoints from 0 to 200B LCCP tokens. This bears on token scaling in a continued-training regime (V5) and on downstream predictability (V6). There are no parameter or compute sweeps.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Hunyuan-A13B needs more than 150B LCCP tokens to saturate, and that NIAH scores show deceptive early saturation while NIAH PPL tracks downstream performance better. They also find retrieval heads are efficient monitors. They state held-out PPL follows PPL = A·log(N)+B, which they call consistent with the scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Measures PPL and downstream benchmark outcomes across one industrial model’s long-context continual-pretraining trajectory; it does not reproduce the original parameter/data/compute scaling-law sweeps or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: PPL evaluation varies by corpus and by NIAH context length and needle depth; the paper states A and B in its empirical PPL formula are associated with architecture and evaluation corpus. It reports diminishing returns at different token amounts across benchmark measures.

fits_no_version.finding: The binary NIAH score correlates with downstream SFT-probe scores (r 0.50 to 0.89) but saturates by 20 to 50B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark proxy metrics can saturate before loss and before downstream capability ('deceptive saturation').

fits_no_version.finding: The count of retrieval heads and their average retrieval score rise with LCCP tokens and correlate with downstream scores (r 0.57 to 0.90; Table 4, Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal attention-head metrics track downstream capability across training checkpoints.

record.problems: Only one model and one LCCP trajectory are studied; PPL trends are primarily shown in figures without tabulated checkpoint values or uncertainty estimates. The paper does not report a direct held-out cross-entropy power-law fit, fitted exponents, or out-of-sample extrapolation tests. Some reported correlations, notably for LongBio, are not statistically significant.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows were omitted. The paper's retrieval-head metrics and their correlations with downstream performance are not included because they do not measure the scaling-law quantities or downstream predictability from scale/loss specified by the versions.

untested.parts: Pretraining from scratch; parameter and compute scaling; power-law fits of held-out loss.
All; no extrapolation from small runs.
All; no comparison of architecture shapes.
Other modalities; repeated data; model-size scaling in continual pretraining; fitted exponents.
Out-of-sample prediction; scaling with parameters or compute; downstream prediction from general held-out PPL (Figure 6 PPL is not correlated with downstream scores).
All; no comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Retrieval-head metrics' correlations with downstream scores, with p-values (not scaling-law quantities, but used as monitors of training progress)

record.verdict_notes: This is a single-model, single-trajectory continual-pretraining study with about 6 checkpoints. The authors' 'consistent with the scaling law' remark rests on a log-linear PPL fit over one decade of tokens; no exponent is fitted. The PPL rows are moved from V1 to V5 because LCCP is a continued-training regime. The NIAH-score correlation rows are unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: Tests PPL against LCCP training tokens in one model; does not test held-out cross-entropy directly, parameter-count or compute scaling, or whether the other quantities are non-bottlenecks.
No fit on small runs followed by prediction or evaluation on much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or comparison of parameter and token growth with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study is about text LCCP; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning scaling, or transfer scaling.
Tests downstream benchmark scores after lightweight SFT and correlations across LCCP checkpoints; does not test broad downstream task families or establish out-of-sample prediction.
No comparison of fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or datasets to test dependence of exponents or compute-optimal splits.

rows.measure: Mean perplexity versus LCCP training tokens
rows.value: figure only; text says mean PPL gradually decreases and is approximately linear with respect to the logarithm of training tokens
rows.note: The paper gives the empirical form PPL = A · log(N) + B, with A and B associated with architecture and corpus. This is a PPL result, not a directly reported cross-entropy loss or a power-law fit.

relationships.condition: Hunyuan-A13B LCCP; held-out Chinese, English and code PPL at 64K, 20B to 200B tokens
relationships.reason: PPL falls with diminishing returns, but the authors fit PPL linear in log tokens rather than a power law. Only one model and about one decade of tokens are covered (R1, R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity decreased with diminishing returns under a fit linear in log tokens, rather than a power law, across one model and about one decade of tokens.

relationships.reason: The probe PPL declines and then plateaus at 150B tokens, bending away from continued smooth improvement (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Answer-token perplexity decreased and then plateaued at 150B tokens.

relationships.condition: MRCR and RULER SFT-probe scores versus LCCP tokens and NIAH PPL
relationships.reason: MRCR improves with tokens (R6), and NIAH PPL correlates significantly with RULER (r=-0.91) and MRCR (r=-0.92) (R12, R13, R15). This rests on about 6 checkpoints and a task-specific loss.
relationships.display_finding: MRCR improved with tokens, while NIAH perplexity correlated with RULER at r=−0.91 and MRCR at r=−0.92 across about six checkpoints.

relationships.reason: RULER saturates after 100B tokens (R5). LongBio shows diminishing returns after 50B (R7), and its correlation with NIAH PPL is not significant (p=0.18, R14).
relationships.display_finding: RULER saturated after 100B tokens, LongBio showed diminishing returns after 50B, and LongBio's correlation with NIAH perplexity was nonsignificant (p=0.18).
